translations.note: The sidenote is anchored at Burton's reference to Pliny. It sums up Pliny, Natural History 7.188 (book 7, chapter 55 in older editions): 'omnibus a supremo die eadem quae ante primum'. It is a paraphrase, not an exact quotation.
translations.text: The same state after death as there was before we were born.

translations.note: Seneca, Letters 54.4, reads 'hoc erit post me quod ante me fuit'. Burton has 'Idem' where Seneca has 'hoc'. In the main text Burton gives the reference as 'lib. 7 epist. 55'; in modern numbering it is letter 54.
translations.text: And Seneca: It will be the same after me as it was before me.

translations.text: from which he infers that it cannot be told which is the truer religion, the Jewish, the Mahometan, or the Christian, since they bear the same marks, etc.

translations.note: Two notorious books. De tribus impostoribus was a legendary treatise, often rumoured and seldom seen. The Cymbalum mundi was by Bonaventure des Périers ('Peresius'). 'He' in 'says he' is Mersenne.
translations.text: On the Three Impostors of the World, which (says he) you cannot read without horror; and the Cymbalum mundi, consisting of four dialogues, printed at Paris in the year 1538, by the author Peresius
